dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing

evidence.note: Genuine environment probing before building: checks python3/node/npm/go/gcc, python version, pip list, installs aiohttp, confirms package availability — establishes real runtime constraints (empty /app, Python 3.12, minimal deps) that steer the architecture choice.
Explicitly verifies the subtle dense-seq-across-writers invariant — confirms IRC PRIVMSG and HTTP POST share a dense per-channel seq (observed 1,2), one of the highest-value contract traps.

Deliberate return to the spec for exact shapes: re-checks coloured sidebar, hashtag channel names, workspace identity, 3-pane layout, /me body kept literally, token length >=16, token storage keys (huddle.token/token/__huddle_token), data-channel-id/name.

Systematically iterates over the full data-testid list to check presence in served HTML, finds only emoji-picker missing and reasons about why (runtime-created) — evidence of distilling the testid contract.

Multiple further spec-reread passes surfacing edge cases (DM idempotency, thread replies oldest-first → ORDER BY id ASC, stable resource ids across cluster, node_id/port mapping, resilience windows 60s/5s) — a living, revisited mental contract map.
Reasons explicitly about resilience windows (supervisor restart <2s vs 60s; fallback poller 1s vs 5s) and IRC port ownership on kill — extracting the resilience invariants from the spec.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it confirms the runtime (language/framework/deps/ports) up front and extracts main contracts per subsystem, catching explicit codes, envelope keys, the testid list, and several genuinely subtle traps (dense-seq-across-writers, /me literal body, token fallback keys, thread oldest-first, resilience timing windows), and it repeatedly returns to the spec (steps 66, 67, 74, 76, 78) rather than coding blind. It falls short of a clean 8 because there is no formal referenced contract inventory and it never surfaces some of the sharpest silent-failure traps the spec plants (guest/member/admin channel gating, non-member mention exclusion, member_user_ids naming, topic-not-auto-populated, transfer-ownership vs PATCH-to-owner). This places it at a 7 — strong, self-correcting contract extraction and environment probing that just misses full coverage of the subtlest gates.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure

evidence.note: Early architecture decision explicitly names the shared substrate as prerequisites: SQLite (WAL) shared store for stable ids + dense seq, and a TCP broadcast hub with a DB-polling fallback for cross-node fan-out. Lays out a layered file plan (db.py → core.py → broadcast.py → app.py → static SPA → start.sh), i.e. foundations before dependents.
Build order is dependency-correct: DB schema first, then core helpers, then broadcast transport, then the full REST API, and only afterward the SPA — API built and verified before UI.

Verification followed the same dependency ladder each with an implicit done-check actually executed: health across 3 nodes → register/login → workspace read → message post → cross-node propagation → IRC → confirming dense seq (1,2) shared across HTTP+IRC writers.

The highest-risk cross-cutting invariants were isolated as their own checks: WS subscribe/head_seq, resume-across-nodes replay, and fan-out survival with the broadcast hub killed (fallback poller within 5s) — the load-bearing resilience milestones treated distinctly.

Plan revised as build revealed new dependencies: recognizing IRC-on-single-node fails under node kill, redesigned start.sh so all nodes race for the IRC port and tested takeover; supervisor/process-supervision treated as a first-class element rather than bolted on.
Course-correction milestone: discovered duplicate WS frames (hub + poller), paused to fix dedup by (channel_id, seq), then re-ran the substrate check — foundation stabilized before moving on.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it produced a sensible, dependency-correct ordered breakdown, recognized the critical shared substrate (dense per-channel seq store, fan-out transport) at the very start, and sequenced foundations before dependents (DB/seq → WS/IRC/resilience; API → SPA). It reaches into anchor 8 territory by making dependencies visible, treating start.sh/supervision as a first-class concern it iterated on, isolating the highest-risk invariants (dense seq across HTTP+IRC, replay-on-reconnect, fan-out survival) as their own verified checks, and revising the design (IRC-on-all-nodes, dedup) as new dependencies surfaced. It falls short of a full 8/10 because the milestones live in prose 'Plan:' fields with executed rather than pre-declared acceptance criteria — no explicit milestone hierarchy — so it lands at 7.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols

evidence.note: Wrote a python IRC socket client (PASS/NICK/USER/JOIN/PRIVMSG) and confirmed the IRC PRIVMSG committed into the same dense per-channel seq stream as HTTP writes (seq 1,2) — verifying the mixed-writer invariant directly.
WebSocket subscribe/replay test found duplicate frames (hub + fallback poller); agent diagnosed, patched dedup by (channel_id, seq), restarted, and re-tested — self-correcting verification.
Actively killed the broadcast hub and verified cross-node fan-out still delivered via the SQLite fallback poller within the 5s window; also ran a cross-node resume test.
SIGKILLed an HTTP node (including the IRC-holding node) and confirmed supervisor restart (~4s, well under 60s) plus IRC port takeover.

Verified pinned data-testid selectors by grepping served HTML rather than driving a real browser; found emoji-picker missing and reasoned about runtime creation — SPA verification remained static, not a browser pass.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built self-directed checks across all four transports, verified the load-bearing invariants directly (dense seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers, WS subscribe/resume, cross-node replay), and — critically — actively simulated both the HTTP-node SIGKILL and broadcast-component kill, confirming continued writes/delivery and seq density within the stated windows; it also used a failed WS test to drive a dedup fix and re-verified. This squarely matches the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because the SPA was only statically grepped for testids (never driven in a browser), edited/deleted/tombstone semantics were not explicitly exercised, and the checks were one-off scripts rather than a single repeatable adversarial harness.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface

evidence.note: Systematically walks subsystems in prose Analysis/Plan fields (auth, workspaces, channels, messages, threads, reactions, DMs, files, search, groups, invitations, WS, IRC, SPA), keeping an implicit running picture of what's built vs. next — but no explicit persistent ledger.

Explicit coverage cross-check: iterates the spec's full testid list against served HTML to find missing selectors, catching emoji-picker and reasoning about why it's runtime-created. This is a genuine cross-check against the contract list to avoid silent drops.

Repeatedly re-enumerates specific remaining spec contracts to verify (/me literal body, token length >=16, data-channel-id, thread reply ordering, DM semantics), showing sustained orientation over the feature surface late in the build.

Noticed duplicate WS frames and fixed dedup; then recognized the supervisor kept restarting the broadcast hub, invalidating the resilience test, and switched to manual node launch — detecting a stuck test state and changing tactics. No genuine circular debugging occurred.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent tracks progress at subsystem granularity and catches most omissions before finishing, including a concrete testid coverage cross-check against the spec's contract list (steps 70-72) and repeated re-enumeration of remaining contracts (steps 66,74,76) — matching and slightly exceeding the level-5 anchor. It falls short of level 8 because it never maintains an explicit, continuously-updated done/partial/failing ledger; coverage tracking is ad-hoc prose, and there was little thrashing to detect (the one stuck-test recognition at steps 50-52 was corrected but not a sustained circular-debugging escape). This places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions

evidence.note: Chose SQLite (WAL) as shared durable store so seq allocation lives in a single durable authority independent of the broadcaster — the exact resilient-sequencing choice the top anchor describes, made proactively at design time.

On discovering duplicate WS frames (hub + poller), diagnosed the root cause (poller re-emitting local writes) and moved dedup to the publish side with a global (channel_id,seq) seen-set — a design-level correction, not a sleep/retry symptom patch.

Proactively stress-tested the broadcast-kill scenario; when supervisor auto-restart masked the test, restructured to run nodes manually without supervisor to genuinely confirm the fallback poller delivers cross-node within the 5s window.
Reasoned ahead that IRC bound only on node 0 would fail on kill, then re-architected so all nodes race to bind IRC and verified takeover after killing the IRC-holding node.
Re-verified the load-bearing invariants after changes: dense shared seq across HTTP+IRC, and cross-node propagation still dense during a broadcast outage.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent proactively stress-tested the risky resilience assumptions early (broadcast-kill, node-kill, IRC takeover) — a level-10 trait — and when reality diverged (duplicate frames, IRC single-node fragility) it treated the failures as design signals, correcting at the right layer (publish-side dedup, all-node IRC binding) and re-verifying seq density and fan-out across the cluster — matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of a clean 10 because the foundational sequencing/transport design was sound from the outset, so the corrections were targeted revisions rather than a dramatic re-architecture of a broken subsystem.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget

evidence.note: Frames the task as 'massive' and front-loads an architecture (shared SQLite + broadcast hub + fallback poller) chosen specifically to satisfy the heavily-graded cross-node resilience/seq invariants — a risk-driven early decision.
Explicit grader-value triage: 'Given the scope, I'll be pragmatic and include only what graders test.'

Weighs the highest-risk graded scenarios (kill node <60s, broadcast-kill <5s fan-out, IRC single-node failover) and adjusts design to protect them — coverage/risk reasoning on load-bearing invariants.
Post-build pass explicitly re-checking the pinned, high-coverage hooks (all testids, token length, token storage keys, seq density, thread ordering) rather than polishing low-value corners.
Conscious 'minimal viable' call: accepts emoji-picker being created at runtime instead of static HTML, reasoning about what the grader actually needs.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent makes explicit grader-coverage statements ('include only what graders test'), front-loads the gating invariants (resilience/seq/testids/token), and makes conscious minimal-viable calls (emoji-picker deferral, single-node IRC failover), which clears anchor 5 and reaches into anchor 8 territory. But it builds nearly the entire feature surface in conventional spec order without sharply deferring low-yield features or running a revisited value/risk allocation across the horizon, so it stops short of 8-10. This places it at 7.

rubric.task_read: A very-long-horizon, multi-subsystem build: a self-contained Slack clone with three HTTP nodes, WebSocket delivery, an IRC gateway, a browser-drivable SPA, and a dense per-channel event sequence that must stay gap-free and fan out across nodes even under SIGKILL of a node or the broadcast component. The spec pins hundreds of exact contracts (status codes, envelopes, IRC numerics, ~80 data-testids, seq invariants, resilience windows). Difficulty comes from enormous breadth, many hard-to-fake distributed-systems invariants, and an opaque grader — so heavy, sustained, well-sequenced meta-work (contract extraction, milestone structure, self-built verification, failure-mode testing) is decisive rather than optional.

dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing
dimensions.description: Mining the dense spec for exact required behaviors (status codes, envelopes, testids, IRC numerics, seq semantics, resilience windows) and probing the runtime (installed tooling, ports, browser) before and during building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader asserts precise shapes across HTTP/WS/IRC/UI; a single mis-read contract (e.g. `member_user_ids` vs `members`, topic not auto-populated from description, seq must advance by exactly 1) silently fails whole check families. Blind coding here guarantees rework.

anchors.0: Starts coding from a vague 'Slack clone' mental model; never returns to the spec for exact shapes; ignores the testid/numeric/seq lists.
anchors.3: Reads the spec once top-to-bottom and codes the obvious CRUD, but misses the sharp edges (auto-#general, role gating, mention exclusion rules, resume.gap, node_id indexing) and never checks what's installed.
anchors.5: Extracts the main contracts per subsystem and confirms the runtime (language/framework/browser/ports) before building; catches most explicit status codes and envelope keys.
anchors.8: Systematically distills the spec into a referenced contract inventory (endpoints, codes, testids, IRC numerics, WS frame kinds, seq/resilience invariants), and probes the environment for real constraints (available ports, Chromium, dependency limits) — surfacing the subtle traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH-to-owner, guest/member/admin channel gates, non-member mention exclusion, dense-seq-across-writers).
anchors.10: Maintains a living, cross-referenced contract map that is revisited as ambiguities surface (e.g. how DM idempotency, tombstoned-reaction counting, or resume.gap boundaries should behave), resolves each under-specified point with an explicit, spec-consistent inference, and lets that research continuously steer implementation order.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the system into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (auth → workspaces/channels → messages/threads/reactions → WS → IRC → SPA → clustering/resilience) each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing them so foundations exist before dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large for one undifferentiated push; without a dependency-aware milestone plan the agent risks building the SPA before the API works or resilience before the seq layer exists, and cannot tell what fraction is truly complete.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between unrelated features reactively; foreground start.sh and clustering treated as afterthoughts.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria; shared foundations (seq store, cross-node transport) not identified as prerequisites.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into major subsystems with rough milestones, each with an implicit 'it works' check; the critical shared substrate (durable per-channel seq, fan-out transport) is recognized early.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance checks, dependencies made visible (auth/token before everything; seq+persistence before WS/IRC/resilience; API before SPA), and start.sh/process-supervision designed as a first-class milestone rather than bolted on.
anchors.10: A crisp, dependency-correct roadmap that isolates the highest-risk cross-cutting invariants (dense seq across HTTP+IRC writers, replay-after-reconnect, fan-out survival) as their own early milestones with concrete exit criteria, sequenced so each later subsystem builds on an already-verified foundation — and the plan is revised as the build reveals new dependencies.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks the grader won't hand you: curl/HTTP assertions on codes and envelopes, WebSocket subscribe/resume/seq tests, IRC socket sessions, SPA driving, and — critically — actively simulating the SIGKILL and broadcast-kill resilience scenarios.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is opaque and covers HTTP+WS+IRC+browser+failure injection. Assuming success is fatal here; only an agent that reproduces the grader's probes (including seq-density-under-partition and replay-on-different-node) can know its work is correct before submission.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'the server starts'; never exercises endpoints, WS frames, IRC, the UI, or any failure scenario.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls on a few happy-path endpoints; UI eyeballed once; resilience and seq-density assumed to work, never tested.
anchors.5: Exercises each subsystem's main paths (HTTP codes, a WS subscribe, an IRC join/privmsg, SPA login/post) and confirms basic error codes, but resilience/fan-out testing is thin or omitted.
anchors.8: Builds reusable checks spanning all four transports, verifies key invariants directly (dense per-channel seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers, resume.gap, cross-node replay), AND actively kills an HTTP node and the broadcast component to confirm continued writes/delivery and seq density within the stated windows.
anchors.10: Runs a comprehensive, repeatable verification harness that mirrors the grader's adversarial probes across nodes and protocols — including node-restart-within-60s, exactly-once fan-out, edited/deleted/tombstone semantics, and a browser pass against the pinned testids — using failures found to drive fixes, and re-verifying end-to-end after changes rather than trusting prior passes.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface
dimensions.description: Keeping an accurate, current picture of which of the many features/contracts are done vs. remaining vs. broken across a long build, and detecting stuck or circular states (e.g. re-debugging seq gaps repeatedly).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of endpoints, ~80 testids, and several invariants, it is easy to lose the plot, silently drop whole feature families, or thrash on one hard bug while the rest rots. Sustained orientation over the horizon is what prevents quitting early with large gaps.

anchors.0: No sense of overall completion; forgets whole subsystems (IRC, search, groups, read-state) or repeats the same failed fix without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; discovers late that major areas were never built; no signal for being stuck.
anchors.5: Tracks progress at subsystem granularity and generally knows what's left, catching most omissions before finishing.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, continuously-updated status of features/contracts (done / partial / failing), notices when a fix isn't converging and names the stuck state, and uses that ledger to decide what to touch next.
anchors.10: Sustains a precise done-vs-remaining map across the entire surface for the whole horizon, cross-checks it against the spec's contract list so nothing is silently dropped, and reliably detects thrashing/circular debugging early enough to switch tactics rather than burn the budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach when reality diverges — e.g. the chosen cross-node transport can't preserve dense seq under the broadcast-kill, or replay-on-different-node exposes a persistence/ordering flaw — instead of pushing ahead on a broken premise.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several requirements (dense seq across nodes+protocols, fan-out survival within 5s of killing the broadcaster, node self-restart) are easy to design wrong on the first try; the difference between success and collapse is whether the agent re-architects when a test falsifies the design.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence; keeps a design that demonstrably violates seq density or resilience and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Patches symptoms locally (retries, sleeps) without questioning a flawed transport/persistence design; recurring failures persist.
anchors.5: When a test fails, diagnoses and makes a targeted correction, occasionally reconsidering a component choice when patches don't hold.
anchors.8: Treats falsified assumptions as design signals: when seq-density or fan-out breaks under failure injection, steps back and revises the sequencing/transport/persistence approach rather than layering hacks, then re-verifies the invariant.
anchors.10: Proactively stress-tests risky design assumptions early, and on divergence performs a clean, reasoned re-architecture of the affected subsystem (e.g. moving seq allocation to a single durable authority so it survives broadcaster loss), documenting why, with minimal collateral damage and full re-verification across the cluster.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget
dimensions.description: Allocating limited effort across a feature set almost too large to complete perfectly — prioritizing the load-bearing, heavily-graded invariants and flows over polish, and consciously deciding what to build first / defer / accept as minimal.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The breadth exceeds what can be perfected; without deliberate triage the agent may over-invest in one polished corner (e.g. slash-command edge cases) while core graded systems (resilience, seq, SPA testids) remain absent. Budget allocation across the horizon materially changes the final score.

anchors.0: No prioritization; effort spent wherever attention lands, leaving high-value subsystems unbuilt while polishing low-value details.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only; over- or under-invests in areas without weighing grader coverage.
anchors.5: Roughly targets the big-ticket, clearly-graded areas first (auth/API/SPA/seq) and leaves minor niceties for later.
anchors.8: Explicitly weighs subsystems by likely grader coverage and risk, front-loads the invariants that gate many checks (token/seq/resilience/testids), and makes conscious 'minimal viable' calls on lower-value features to protect the whole.
anchors.10: Runs a deliberate, revisited value/risk allocation across the full horizon — sequencing so the highest-coverage, highest-risk systems are solid early, deferring or stubbing low-yield features intentionally, and reallocating budget as verification reveals where marginal effort buys the most score.
